content: Stakeholders from 43 countries, including 20 high-income and 23 lowand middle-income nations, provided substantial support for targeted testing of specific populations. These populations included blood donors (over 85%), children born to mothers infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV) (75%), individuals living with HIV (65%), pregnant women (78%), men who have sex with men (MSM) (45%), sex workers (45%), prisoners (25%), and those with chronic illnesses (approximately 25%). However, general population testing for HBV infection was supported by only one-third of respondents. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the impact and cost-effectiveness of different hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing approaches, such as general population testing or focused testing, was limited by the small number of available studies and the heterogeneity of settings, populations, and measured outcomes. Consequently, a narrative review was conducted, incorporating recent systematic reviews of HCV seroprevalence in various populations. The three main testing strategies evaluated were: (i) routine testing across the entire population, (ii) focused or targeted testing of high-risk groups, and (iii) routine testing among specific birth cohorts. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low. Most studies originated from Europe or the United States, with very few from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Fourteen studies assessed general population testing, 13 focused on people who inject drugs (PWID) and sexually transmitted disease (STD) clinics, three on blood transfusion recipients, one on HIV-infected MSM, two on pregnant women, and two on other populations. Focused testing of PWID, individuals in prisons or closed settings, and HIV-infected MSM was found to be cost-effective in all settings, even when studies assumed poor follow-up rates, limited access to therapy, and a high risk of reinfection. Higher treatment rates were associated with greater population impact and improved cost-effectiveness of HCV case-finding. Among prisoners, targeting those with a history of injection drug use further enhanced cost-effectiveness. For HIV-positive MSM, cost-effectiveness depended on effective linkage to therapy and retention in care. Birth-cohort testing, which targets easily identifiable age or demographic groups with higher HCV prevalence, was shown to be cost-effective in studies from the United States and Portugal when compared to risk-based screening or current testing approaches. Routine testing in the general population was generally not cost-effective outside of high-prevalence settings. A major limitation of existing cost-effectiveness studies was their reliance on interferon-based regimens rather than newer direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatments. Only one cost-effectiveness study was conducted in an LMIC, specifically in Egypt, which has a very high disease prevalence. Routine testing was shown to be cost-effective even when treatment was based on pegylated interferon and ribavirin. The cost-effectiveness of testing strategies was influenced by factors such as the replacement of interferon-based regimens with more effective DAAs, progression rates from chronic HCV to cirrhosis, and levels of linkage to care and treatment. Screening and treatment costs had relatively little impact on cost-effectiveness. Based on a narrative review of heterogeneous studies from high-income countries, the overall quality of evidence was rated as low. The Guidelines Development Group recognized the heterogeneity of HCV epidemics worldwide, which are often a mix of three main patterns: (1) infection related to high-risk behaviors, requiring focused testing in high-risk groups; (2) a birth cohort epidemic, requiring routine testing among specific birth cohorts with high HCV prevalence; and (3) a generalized population epidemic with high prevalence due to widespread, often iatrogenic, exposure, requiring routine testing across the entire population. Most countries have mixed epidemic profiles, and the optimal testing strategy depends on the unique HCV epidemiology of each country. Testing in high-risk groups such as PWID, MSM, prisoners, HIV-infected individuals, and sex workers was cost-effective in all settings. Birth-cohort testing is likely to be cost-effective in most settings, while routine population screening may not be cost-effective in most epidemic settings. Focused risk-based testing was recommended for populations at the highest risk of acquiring and transmitting HCV, such as PWID, prisoners, MSM, and sex workers, as it is both cost-effective and yields a high rate of case detection. Other high-risk groups for focused testing include individuals with tattoos, body piercings, or scarification, those who underwent unsafe medical procedures, recipients of unscreened blood products, and close contacts of HCV-infected individuals. Screening was also recommended for children born to HCV-infected mothers, particularly if the mother is also HIV-infected, due to the increased risk of mother-to-child transmission. Community-based testing strategies, such as door-to-door testing, mobile outreach campaigns, and testing in workplaces, parks, bars, places of worship, and educational institutions, can increase the acceptance and uptake of testing, particularly among first-time testers and those who rarely use clinical services. Community-based testing is especially beneficial for key and vulnerable populations and asymptomatic individuals. Innovative models of care, such as integrated HIV and hepatitis testing and opioid substitution therapy for PWID, have been successfully implemented in many settings. However, challenges include ensuring access to prevention, care, and treatment services, as well as addressing potential confidentiality breaches, stigma, and discrimination. Facility-based testing for viral hepatitis in high-risk populations provides an opportunity to scale up testing and can be integrated with other health services, such as HIV testing and treatment. This approach is generally associated with higher case identification rates and greater cost-effectiveness. However, in low-prevalence settings, routine facility-based testing is likely to be cost-effective only for high-risk populations.
